newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Canadian billionaire bets store on Hungarian mall.
newsitem.headline: Canadian billionaire bets store on Hungarian mall.

text.p: Canadian billionaire Peter Munk has opened central Europe's biggest shopping mall on a hunch that people will change the way they shop.

"This region is a large business opportunity," Munk said during a visit to Hungary for the inauguration of the vast Polus Centre, built on the grounds of a former Soviet army barracks on the outskirts of Budapest.

With an ice-skating rink, theatre, restaurants, banks, shop and interiors imitating a 19th century town on the American prairie, the $120 million mall almost goes overboard in being stridently un-Hungarian.
"Hungarian shops are not modern ... transportation and storage costs too much," said Sandor Demjan, the lead Hungarian investor in the project.
He said despite the huge capital investment, the big stores at Polus will be able to undercut smaller competitors.
"At a size like (Polus) costs can be cut by 10 percent," he said of the 602,800 square foot mall.
"A revolution is going on in trade (in the region)," Demjan added. "Traders who do not set up in these shopping centres will be in a difficult situation."

Hungarian-born Munk, opened the mall on his 68th birthday, two days after receiving the 1996 Distinguished Leadership Award at the New York Mercantile Exchange. He said the move was strictly business and denied he had invested in Hungary for sentimental reasons.
Munk left Hungary in 1944, a year before it fell to Soviet troops importing a communist system which maimed the economy for decades.
"For the last 50 years, this site was occupied by a Soviet army barracks, whose soldiers were in Hungary preserving the power of the Soviet Empire," Munk said in a speech.
But Hungary was the first country to demolish in 1989 a part of the Iron Curtain dividing Europe during the Cold War and is rapidly building a market economy.
Hungary joined the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development in March, and wants to boost its economy and be among the frontrunners to join the European Union around 2000.

Parallel with Hungary's reforms, Munk has emerged as the owner of one of the world's largest gold and real estate groups since the 1980s and hopes to expand its empire further in the next 10 years, with Hungary being a part of his plans.

"With our exceptional financial strength, strategic vision and real estate expertise (the real estate group controlled by Munk) Trizec Hahn is now pursuing an aggressive growth strategy in Central Europe," Munk said.

Munk controls Canada's Barrick Gold Corp., the world's largest gold producer outside South Africa, and Trizec Hahn, the second largest real estate firm in North America, both of which have a strategy of rapid global expansion.
The Polus Centre was built by Hungarian and Canadian investors, grouping around Munk and including another Hungarian-born Canadian, Andrew Sarlos, and Demjan.
The mall, which is of a size never seen before in the region, was built in only 344 days, which the builders said was a record for a project of its size.

The builders plan some 25 malls in central Europe over the next seven years, exploiting changing customer habits in a region where only 3 percent of retail trade goes through shopping centres -- compared with 50 percent in Western countries and 70 percent in the United States.
Demjan said the plans, which are worth $3 billion, include building modern offices and industrial parks.
Earlier this year, Munk's companies took part in the construction of an industrial park on the outskirts of Berlin, and Hungary's first modern banking office centre in Budapest.

Munk said that Trizec Hahn, which was set on a strong growth pattern, had identified the Central European area as one of its three geographical priority areas for investments, which also include southeast Asia and Latin America.
